content.thinking:
The alarm was fitted in April 2019 with a 7-year lifespan, so it's due to expire in 2026—still within range but the chirping pattern (once a minute since last night) strongly suggests end-of-life or fault rather than active CO detection, especially since it has a sealed battery the tenant can't replace. Still, I can't rule out genuine CO danger just because a chirp usually signals fault, so safety has to come first: advise ventilating the space, and if anyone shows symptoms, leave immediately and call 999.

Since the battery is sealed, replacement falls to the landlord, not the tenant—clause 12.8 about tenant-replaceable batteries doesn't apply here, and the gas boiler on-site raises the urgency. This is well within the £300 spend limit and should be treated as urgent, so I need to check existing tickets before creating a new one, and note the tenant's contact details since the call dropped but there's an SMS number on file.

arguments.body: Hi Priya, sorry our call dropped. Your CO alarm is a sealed unit fitted in 2019 and is past its 7-year life, so the chirp is most likely it reaching end of life. Please don't take the battery out or cover it (it's sealed anyway), and don't assume it's harmless. Open a window for fresh air. If anyone has a headache, dizziness, nausea or feels drowsy, or the alarm goes into a continuous loud alarm, leave the flat, call 999, and call the Gas Emergency line on 0800 111 999. We've logged this as urgent (JOB-101) and are arranging a replacement alarm and a check, target within 72 hours; we'll update you. Replacing a sealed alarm is the landlord's job, not yours. We've also logged the noisy bathroom fan separately (JOB-102) as routine.
